title: Breath Prayer
subtitle: Slow breathing with Psalm 46:10
summary: Pair slow, steady breathing with a short line of Scripture to calm your body and center your heart on God.
steps: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop.
Breathe in gently through your nose for 4 seconds, praying, “Be still…”
Breathe out slowly for 6 seconds, praying, “…and know that I am God.”
Continue for a few minutes. When your mind wanders, gently return to the words.
verse: Be still and know that I am God
evidence: Slow breathing at around six breaths per minute is associated with greater heart-rate variability, relaxation, and lower anxiety.

title: Cyclic Sighing
subtitle: A double inhale and a long, slow exhale
summary: An exhale-focused breathing pattern that quickly settles your nervous system. Remember that every breath is a gift from God.
steps: Breathe in through your nose until your lungs are nearly full.
Take a second, shorter sip of air to fill them completely.
Exhale slowly and fully through your mouth — make the exhale longer than the inhales.
Repeat for about five minutes, at a relaxed pace.
verse: the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being.
evidence: In a one-month randomized study, five minutes a day of cyclic sighing improved positive mood more than mindfulness meditation and reduced breathing rate.

title: Three Good Things
subtitle: A gratitude journal for tonight
summary: Write down three things that went well today and why. It trains your attention to notice God's kindness.
steps: Think back over your day.
Write down three things that went well — big or small.
For each one, write why it happened or what it meant to you.
Thank God for each one.
prompts: First good thing — and why it happened:
Second good thing — and why it happened:
Third good thing — and why it happened:
verse: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds
evidence: Writing down three things that went well each day, and why, increased happiness and reduced depressive symptoms for up to six months in a randomized trial.

title: Gratitude Letter
subtitle: Thank someone who made a difference
summary: Write a letter to someone you have never properly thanked. Share it with them if you can.
steps: Think of someone whose kindness changed your life.
Write to them specifically: what they did and how it affected you.
If you can, deliver it in person or read it to them.
Pray a blessing over them.
verse: I thank my God every time I remember you.
evidence: Writing and delivering a gratitude letter produced one of the largest short-term boosts in happiness in a randomized trial, strongest over the following month.

title: Acts of Kindness
subtitle: Plan a few kind acts for one day
summary: Choose a day and plan a few intentional acts of kindness. Love in action blesses the giver, too.
steps: Pick a day this week.
Plan up to five kind acts — simple is fine.
Do them, and notice how you feel.
Thank God for the chance to love others.
checklist: Encourage someone with a specific compliment
Help with a task without being asked
Pray for someone and let them know
verse: It is more blessed to give than to receive.
evidence: Performing acts of kindness reliably increases the giver's well-being; several acts in a single day may give a bigger boost than spreading them out.

title: Savoring Walk
subtitle: Taste and see what is good
summary: Take a short walk and deliberately notice and linger on good things — light, color, sound, kindness.
steps: Walk somewhere pleasant, at an easy pace.
Look for as many good things as you can: beauty, warmth, small joys.
When you notice one, pause and let yourself enjoy it.
Thank God for each gift you notice.
verse: Taste and see that the LORD is good
evidence: Savoring — noticing and lingering on positive moments — is linked to greater happiness; a daily savoring walk raised happiness in a study of students.

title: Best Possible Self
subtitle: Write a hopeful vision
summary: Imagine your life in the future after things have gone as well as they reasonably could, and write it down with God's purposes in mind.
steps: Picture yourself a few years from now, after things have gone well.
Write about your relationships, faith, work, and health in that future.
Be realistic and hopeful — this is about what could be, by God's grace.
Note one small step you could take toward it this week.
prompts: One small step I can take this week:
verse: Write down this vision and clearly inscribe it on tablets
evidence: Writing about your best possible future self increases optimism and positive mood, supported by a meta-analysis of optimism interventions.

title: Self-Compassion Break
subtitle: Receive the gentleness of Jesus
summary: Meet your own pain with the kindness Jesus shows you, instead of harsh self-criticism.
steps: Name it honestly: “This is a moment of suffering.” Jesus noticed pain, too.
Remember you are not alone: “Others feel this way. Struggle is part of being human.”
Place a hand over your heart and pray: “Lord, help me be as gentle with myself as You are with me.”
Ask: “What would Jesus say to me right now?” Let yourself hear it.
verse: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.
evidence: Self-compassion training reduces anxiety, depression, and stress and increases life satisfaction across randomized trials.

title: Move Your Body
subtitle: A walk, a stretch, a dance
summary: Get your body moving at a pace that feels good. Caring for your body honors the One who made it.
steps: Choose any movement you enjoy — walking is great.
Aim for a comfortable effort where you can still talk.
If you can, go outside.
Afterward, notice how your mood and energy have changed.
verse: Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God?
evidence: Physical activity, including walking, meaningfully reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety. Adults are advised to get 150–300 minutes of moderate activity each week.

title: Consider the Lilies
subtitle: Time in God's creation
summary: Spend unhurried time outdoors — a park, a garden, the sky — noticing God's care in creation.
steps: Find a green or open space, even a small one.
Slow down and notice plants, birds, sky, and light.
Remember Jesus' words: your Father cares for these — and for you.
Leave your phone in your pocket if you can.
verse: Consider how the lilies of the field grow
evidence: People who spend at least 120 minutes a week in nature are more likely to report good health and well-being, and a nature walk reduced rumination compared with an urban walk.

title: Reach Out
subtitle: Connect with someone today
summary: Send a message, make a call, or plan a visit with someone you trust. You were not made to do life alone.
steps: Think of one person you trust or miss.
Send a short message, call, or invite them to meet.
If you're struggling, tell them honestly — let them carry some of the weight.
Thank God for the people He has given you.
verse: Two are better than one
evidence: Strong social relationships are linked to a 50% greater likelihood of survival over time, an effect comparable to quitting smoking.

title: Sleep Wind-Down
subtitle: Hand the night to God
summary: A gentle routine to prepare your body and mind for rest.
steps: Work through the checklist in the hour before bed.
Write tomorrow's worries down so your mind can let them go.
Pray Psalm 4:8 as you lie down.
checklist: Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time
Dim the lights and put screens away 30–60 minutes before bed
Avoid caffeine late in the day
Write down tomorrow's worries and hand them to God
Pray Psalm 4:8 as you lie down
verse: I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.
evidence: Adults need seven or more hours of sleep for good health. Consistent habits, such as a regular schedule and limiting late caffeine, support better sleep.

title: Lament & Expressive Writing
subtitle: Pour out your heart
summary: Write honestly about what you're feeling and why, the way the psalmists did. God can handle your honesty.
steps: Set a timer for 15 minutes.
Write your deepest thoughts and feelings about what is troubling you — don't edit.
Tell God exactly how it feels, like the lament psalms do.
End by writing one thing you trust God with.
prompts: What I want to tell God:
One thing I trust You with:
verse: Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him. God is our refuge.
evidence: Writing about your deepest thoughts and feelings for about 15 minutes on a few occasions has small but reliable benefits for health and well-being.

title: Scripture Meditation
subtitle: Slowly savor a verse
summary: Read a short passage slowly, repeat a phrase, and let it sink in — meditation the biblical way.
steps: Read today's verse slowly, out loud if you can.
Read it again and notice a word or phrase that stands out.
Repeat that phrase quietly to yourself — the Hebrew word for meditate means to murmur.
Respond to God in prayer, then rest in silence for a minute.
verse: But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night.
evidence: Religiously integrated CBT, which includes reflecting on Scripture, was as effective as conventional CBT for depression in a randomized trial, and faith-adapted therapies work well for many believers.

title: Daily Examen
subtitle: Review your day with God
summary: A centuries-old prayer of reflection: notice God's presence, give thanks, and look ahead with hope.
steps: Become aware of God's presence with you now.
Review your day with gratitude — what were the gifts?
Notice your emotions: what drew you toward God, and what pulled you away?
Choose one moment from the day and pray about it.
Look toward tomorrow and ask God for what you need.
verse: Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns. See if there is any offensive way in me; lead me in the way everlasting.
evidence: The Examen combines gratitude and honest reflection — practices linked with greater well-being.

title: One Small Step
subtitle: Act first; feelings often follow
summary: When you feel low, choose one small, meaningful activity and do it — even before you feel like it.
steps: Pick one small activity that matters to you: a walk, a call, tidying a corner, a hobby.
Make it tiny — 5 to 10 minutes.
Do it, even if you don't feel like it yet. Motivation often follows action.
Notice how you feel afterward. Rest and food count, too — just ask Elijah.
verse: Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.
evidence: Behavioral activation — scheduling small, meaningful activities — is an effective, well-established treatment for depression.

title: Use Your Gifts
subtitle: A strength in a new way
summary: Identify one of your God-given strengths and use it in a new way today.
steps: Name a strength others see in you (kindness, creativity, courage, humor, wisdom…).
Choose a new way to use it today, especially to serve someone.
Do it.
Reflect on how it felt to use what God has given you.
prompts: A new way I'll use it today:
verse: We have different gifts according to the grace given us.
evidence: Using a signature strength in a new way each day for a week increased happiness and reduced depressive symptoms for six months in a randomized trial.

title: Forgiveness Steps
subtitle: The REACH model with Christ
summary: A structured, research-based path toward releasing resentment — without excusing harm or ignoring safety.
steps: Recall the hurt honestly, without minimizing it.
Empathize: try to understand what might have been going on for the other person — this is not excusing it.
Altruistic gift: remember a time you were forgiven, and consider offering forgiveness as a gift.
Commit: write a note to yourself about your decision to begin forgiving.
Hold on: when the memory returns, remember your decision. Forgiveness is not reconciliation, and if you are unsafe, your safety comes first.
verse: Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.
evidence: Structured forgiveness interventions increase forgiveness and hope and reduce depression and anxiety, according to a meta-analysis.

title: Sabbath Pause
subtitle: Rest as a rhythm, not a reward
summary: Set aside unhurried time to stop working, rest, and enjoy God and the people you love.
steps: Choose a block of time to stop work and productivity.
Do something restful and life-giving — a walk, a meal with friends, worship, a nap.
Put away work messages if you can.
Thank God that your worth isn't measured by your output.
verse: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
evidence: Mentally detaching from work and enjoying restful activities during time off is linked with better well-being and less exhaustion.

title: 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding
subtitle: Come back to the present moment
summary: When anxiety or panic surges, use your senses to anchor yourself in the present, where God is with you.
steps: Name 5 things you can see.
Name 4 things you can feel.
Name 3 things you can hear.
Name 2 things you can smell.
Name 1 thing you can taste — and one truth: God is with you right now.
verse: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.
evidence: Grounding is a widely used clinical coping skill that anchors attention in the present; it draws on the same attention-training principles as mindfulness, which reduces anxiety.
